title: The deal that doubled orders
units_note: All money figures in ₹ lakh unless marked. Costs and deductions are shown in brackets, e.g. (280).

brief.headline: Sales up 25%. Biggest customer up 55%. Now losing money.
brief.story: FreshFarm buys fruit and vegetables at the mandi every morning and supplies quick-commerce dark stores and restaurants across Bengaluru. In July it signed new terms with ZipCart, its biggest customer, and ZipCart's orders jumped 55%. The quarter still ended in a loss. The founder blames the monsoon spike in tomato prices and wants to raise rates across the board.

causes.label: Mandi prices rose in the monsoon
causes.feedback: Prices rose about 3% overall; purchases went from 70% to 71% of sales, roughly ₹5L. Not ₹42L.

causes.label: A new sale-or-return deal lets the biggest customer charge back everything it doesn't sell, and it is over-ordering

causes.feedback: Dock rejections moved from 1.1% to 1.2%, and they're counted in own wastage, which fell.

causes.feedback: ZipCart pays on day 30, every time. Late payment would hit cash, not profit.

causes.feedback: Minutely dipped ₹5L in sales. Small, and those sales are firm.

causes.feedback: ZipCart is on the same price list as before.

causes.feedback: Produce still sits 1.2 days in FreshFarm's warehouse. The overstock is at ZipCart's dark stores, at FreshFarm's expense.

causes.feedback: TDS is 0.1%, shown separately, and isn't a cost.

causes.feedback: Prices didn't change. ZipCart got something more expensive: the right to send back what it doesn't sell.

causes.label: The tomato price spike
causes.feedback: Tomatoes rose ₹4 a kg, but they're one item. All purchases together rose about 3%.

bonus.question: What should the founder push ZipCart for first?
options: A 15% price increase on everything ZipCart buys
End sale-or-return, or cap returns at about 3% of orders with FreshFarm setting the quantities
Faster payment, in 15 days instead of 30
bonus.explanation: Under sale-or-return, ZipCart orders generously because unsold stock costs it nothing; FreshFarm pays for every crate it doesn't sell. Capping or removing returns makes ZipCart order what it can sell. A price rise doesn't fix over-ordering, and faster payment helps cash, not profit.

explanation.answer: From 1 July ZipCart buys on sale-or-return and sets its own order quantities. It ordered 55% more but sold only 81.6% of it, and charged back the rest at invoice value. ZipCart's chargebacks jumped from ₹3L to ₹57L, and FreshFarm still paid for the produce and its transport. The ₹54L jump in chargebacks is more than the whole ₹42L swing into loss.
fastest_path: Open the P&L. Chargebacks for unsold stock jumped from ₹8L to ₹62L; everything else moved with volume.
Open deductions by customer. Almost all of it is ZipCart: ₹57L.
Open customer terms. ZipCart moved to sale-or-return on 1 July, and it decides how much to order.
traps: ZipCart's 55% growth is the misleading number: much of it was stock that came back.
The tomato spike and monsoon mandi prices are the founder's story, and they're in the team chat every day. Overall they added about ₹5L.
"FreshFarm is overstocking" is the near-miss: the overstock sits in ZipCart's dark stores, and FreshFarm pays for it.
explanation.lesson: Revenue a customer can send back isn't revenue yet.
